newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's phone companies brace for new rules.
newsitem.headline: Canada's phone companies brace for new rules.

text.p: Canada's telephone companies were braced for new government regulations expected on Thursday that would allow competition in local phone services across the country.

The Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommuications Commission (CRTC), a federal regulatory body based in Ottawa, was set to unveil new rules on competition and pricing in the local telephone services market.

The rules will represent the second and perhaps last major step in the deregulation of Canada's telecommunications market, said officials at Montreal-based BCE Inc., which owns Bell Canada, the country's biggest telephone company.
"I am hoping for a balanced view," John McLennan, chief executive officer of Bell Canada, told reporters after BCE's annual meeting.

McLennan said that among other issues, the CRTC is expected to set the terms under which Canada's domestic telephone companies will make their local networks available to foreign concerns such as AT&T Corp., Sprint Corp., and to other telephone service resellers.
The CRTC also will establish a new pricing structure for local phone rates.

McLennan said that each year, Bell Canada, which operates a telephone network serving 7 million residential and business customers in Ontario and Quebec, Canada's two most populated provinces, absorbs a more than C$1 billion ($730 million) deficit from operating local services in Canada.
That deficit is offset by profits from long-distance, business and other services. Bell Canada has said it expects a net profit of C$850 million ($620 million) in 1997.

Canada deregulated its long-distance market in 1994, allowing resellers to enter the Canadian market. As a result, Bell Canada's share of the long-distance market slipped from a virtual monopoly to under 70 percent in 1996.
That decline provoked a three-year restructuring programme at Bell Canada under which it will have cut 10,000 jobs by the end of this year.

McLennan said Bell Canada is concerned that under the new CRTC regulations, competitors will be able to piggyback on the company's local networks at low cost, while maintaining their aggressive pricing policy on long-distance rates.
That would leave Bell Canada and other members of Canada's Stentor group of phone companies with few options to find new growth markets.
"When we make our local networks available, we don't get anything new," McLennan said.

Mclennan said he expects that under the new CRTC rules, local services competition will be quite brisk in profitable, high density urban areas, and prices charged to customers there will likely come down over time.
But Bell Canada and other domestic companies that are required to provide local services to rural areas may have to increase prices for those customers, he said.
